name: Comparing forecasts: tests of equal predictive accuracy and dependence-aware resampling. Core: Diebold & Mariano (1995), 'Comparing Predictive Accuracy' (JBES 13(3):253-263); Harvey, Leybourne & Newbold (1997), 'Testing the equality of prediction mean squared errors' (IJF 13(2):281-291); Giacomini & White (2006), 'Tests of Conditional Predictive Ability' (Econometrica 74(6):1545-1578); Diebold (2015), 'Comparing Predictive Accuracy, Twenty Years Later: A Personal Perspective on the Use and Abuse of Diebold-Mariano Tests' (JBES 33(1)). Resampling: Kuensch (1989) moving-block bootstrap; Politis & Romano (1994) stationary bootstrap; Politis & White (2004) automatic block length, corrected by Patton, Politis & White (2009). Panel / spatial / verification extensions: Qu, Timmermann & Zhu (2024), 'Comparing forecasting performance with panel data' (IJF 40(3):918-941); Hering & Genton (2011), 'Comparing spatial predictions' (Technometrics 53(4):414-425); Gilleland, Hering, Fowler & Brown (2018), 'Testing the tests' (MWR 146(6):1685-1703); DelSole & Tippett (2014, 2016) skill-comparison and random-walk/sign tests; Coroneo & Iacone (2020) fixed-smoothing DM. Multiple comparisons: Hansen (2005) SPA test; Hansen, Lunde & Nason (2011) Model Confidence Set. Related caveats: Clark & West (2007) nested models; Lerch et al. (2017) forecaster's dilemma.
type: method family (statistical inference on forecast-score differences: DM-type t tests with HAC variance, conditional predictive ability tests, block/stationary bootstrap of score differences, panel and spatial variants, multiple-comparison corrections)

popularity: Diebold & Mariano 1995 is among the most cited papers in forecasting (order of 10,000+ citations) [uncertain: count not re-checked today]. Giacomini & White 2006 several thousand citations [uncertain]. Politis & Romano 1994 several thousand [uncertain]. Hansen-Lunde-Nason MCS and Hansen SPA each well over a thousand [uncertain]. Panel DM (2024) is recent with few citations. Gilleland et al. 2018 is a standard reference in meteorological verification. DM is implemented in statsmodels, R forecast, R verification, GAUSS, and the Python 'scores' package; arch provides stationary/circular/moving block bootstraps, optimal_block_length, SPA, StepM and MCS.
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed (JBES, IJF, Econometrica, JASA, Annals of Statistics, Econometric Reviews, Technometrics, MWR, J. Applied Econometrics, J. Econometrics, Statistical Science). The illustrative numbers computed for our project in this entry (see headline_results) are this researcher's own unreviewed computation on already-scored predictions, not a pipeline output.
target_type: Not a forecasting application: the methods test whether the expected loss of two forecasts differs, for any target. They apply directly to our onset target with Brier loss, d_it = (p_model,it - y_it)^2 - (p_recent,it - y_it)^2. Like proper scores, they do not protect against a state target: a state target with strong persistence would give a large and 'significant' gain over a weak baseline. The test is only as meaningful as the target and the at-risk mask fixed beforehand (CLAUDE.md Target).
target_definition: Generic: null H0: E[d_t] = 0 (DM, unconditional equal predictive accuracy), or H0: E[d_{t+1} | F_t] = 0 (GW, conditional: no information known at t predicts which forecast will win). For us: y(t) = 1 if a new alert starts in (t, t+1h], per oblast-hour, forecast at the start of the hour; loss = Brier; d < 0 means the model beats the rolling recent-rate baseline. Since H = 1, the label of row t is known at t+1h, so the GW instruments may use d up to t-1h. For H = 3 (official_h3), d is serially correlated by construction (overlapping label windows), so the HAC lag must be at least H-1 even without clustering.
spatial_unit: Not applicable to the papers; DM is for a single series. For our panel (24 units x hours) the right resampling/variance unit is the TIME CLUSTER (one forecast hour across all 24 units, or one day / one week across all units), because mass attacks create a common component in d across oblasts. The panel DM paper (Qu, Timmermann & Zhu 2024) shows that a strong common component invalidates a cross-sectional CLT over units. Hering & Genton 2011 and Gilleland et al. 2018 treat the spatial-field case.
at_risk_masking: Not addressed in the papers, but it matters for validity. The DM statistic must be computed on the IDENTICAL row set for both forecasts (same at-risk mask, gap mask, feature-availability mask). Masking on 'under alert at t' is conditioning on information known at t, which is allowed (it is a GW-style conditioning set). Restricting the evaluation set by the OUTCOME (e.g. only hours with onsets, or 'busy days' chosen after the fact) is the forecaster's dilemma (Lerch et al. 2017) and makes the comparison improper. Masking makes the hourly cluster sizes uneven (N_t ranges up to 24), so the statistic should be a ratio of sums, linearised as u_t = (D_t - dbar * N_t) / Nbar, not a plain mean of per-hour means.
data_sources: Papers: DM and HLN use simulated and macro/financial series; GW use macro forecasts (US data); panel DM uses IMF World Economic Outlook vs private-sector survey forecasts of country GDP growth and inflation; Hering-Genton use wind speed fields [uncertain: application details not re-checked]; Gilleland et al. simulate correlated competing forecast series; DelSole-Tippett use seasonal climate forecasts; Coroneo-Iacone use US SPF and ECB SPF vs a random walk. Our illustrative check (this entry) used reports/official/test_predictions.csv: frozen headline model vs rolling recent-rate on the official test window.
data_source_variant: Not applicable to the papers. Our check: official source only (D-007), H = 1, target_levels = any, 13,116 scored rows. Important finding: although the test window is nominally 2026-07-27 -> 2026-09-07 (6 weeks), scored rows only span 2026-07-27 00:00 -> 2026-08-28 22:00 UTC: 791 forecast hours, 33 days, 5 calendar-week blocks (the last one partial, 1,898 rows). The rest is gap_or_missing (3,480 rows) or feature_missing (1,199 rows, features whose lookback crosses the 29 Aug - 2 Sep gap), plus 6,397 under_alert rows. So the effective test length for inference is about 4.7 weeks, not 6.
preprocessing: Method-level: (1) Form the loss differential per row on the shared eligible set. (2) Aggregate to time clusters: per forecast hour, D_t = sum over units of d_it, N_t = number of scored units. (3) Estimate the long-run variance of the cluster series with a HAC kernel (Newey-West/Bartlett), or resample whole time blocks. (4) For small numbers of blocks, use small-sample corrections (HLN t with T-1 df) or fixed-smoothing (fixed-b) critical values (Coroneo & Iacone 2020). (5) Choose block length by a rule fixed in advance (e.g. 24h for daily attack cycles, plus 72h and 168h as sensitivity), or Politis-White with the 2009 correction (arch.bootstrap.optimal_block_length).
known_label_artefacts: Not applicable to the papers. Artefacts that affect inference in our setting: (a) Mass-attack hours produce simultaneous onsets in many oblasts, i.e. cross-sectional dependence in d; iid-over-rows inference treats one mass attack as many independent trials. (b) The recording gap (29 Aug - 2 Sep) and its feature-missing tail cut the last week, leaving 5 uneven week-blocks; a week-block bootstrap on 5 blocks has only 5^5 = 3,125 distinct resamples and a lumpy percentile distribution. (c) The rolling recent-rate baseline and the model share inputs (both depend on recent onsets), so their errors are positively correlated; this is exactly why a PAIRED test on d is needed and why comparing two separate CIs is wrong (DelSole & Tippett 2014; Gilleland et al. 2018). (d) Standing-alert cap (D-020) and at-risk mask shift which rows are scored; any re-masking changes d and must be identical for both forecasts.
model_family: Inference procedures, not models. (1) DM: t = dbar / sqrt(LRV_hat / T), LRV via HAC (Bartlett/Newey-West), asymptotically N(0,1) under covariance stationarity of d; designed to compare FORECASTS treated as primitives (Diebold 2015), not to test which population model is better. (2) HLN: multiply DM by sqrt((T + 1 - 2h + h(h-1)/T) / T) and use Student t(T-1); reduces over-rejection in small samples and multi-step horizons. (3) GW: Wald test that E[h_t d_{t+1}] = 0 for instruments h_t known at t (constant + e.g. recent activity level, lagged loss differential); valid with rolling/fixed estimation windows and nested or non-nested models, because it targets forecasts produced by a given estimation method, including estimation noise; a later critique (Zhu & Timmermann 2020) argues the GW null cannot hold under rolling windows and that it can be size-distorted for unconditional tests. (4) Block bootstraps: moving-block (Kuensch 1989), circular, stationary (Politis-Romano 1994, random geometric block lengths); resample time blocks of the paired differential (or of paired losses, to get a CI for the BSS ratio). (5) Panel DM (Qu-Timmermann-Zhu 2024): tests pooled over units and time, over subsets of time periods, or clusters of units; handles common factors in loss differentials. (6) Spatial/verification: Hering-Genton fit a parametric autocovariance to d to stabilise the LRV, and were the most robust test under both temporal and between-model correlation in Gilleland et al. 2018; DelSole-Tippett random-walk/sign test counts wins and is distribution-free but loses power and is only partially robust to serial correlation. (7) Multiple comparisons: Hansen SPA (is any competitor better than the benchmark?) and the MCS (set of forecasts containing the best with given confidence), both via stationary bootstrap. (8) Nested models: Clark-West adjustment.
features: Not applicable (no forecasting features). Method components relevant to us: the loss function (Brier, the PRIMARY metric's building block; DM works for any loss, including log loss with clipping); the HAC lag/bandwidth (L = 0, 6, 24, 72, 168 hours tried in our check); block length (24h, 72h, 168h, stationary mean 24h, calendar day, calendar week); GW instruments known at t (mean recent-rate level across units, model-baseline disagreement p_model - p_recent, rolling 24h mean of past d). Python options without new dependencies: numpy/scipy are enough (our check used only the pinned venv: numpy 2.5.4, pandas 3.0.6, scipy 1.18.1). statsmodels and arch are NOT in the project venv; adding them requires the human's approval (CLAUDE.md).
external_feature_timing: Not applicable. Timing rule for GW instruments: every instrument must be known at forecast time t. With H = 1 the loss of row t-1h is known at t, so lagged d up to t-1h is legitimate; with H = 3 only d up to t-3h. Using the CURRENT hour's realised national onset count as a conditioning variable would condition on the outcome (forecaster's dilemma), not on information.
ablation_design: DM/bootstrap tests are the right tool for ablations evaluated on the same rows: each feature block vs the base model gives a paired d series. But many ablations or variants compared on the same test set create a multiple-testing / data-snooping problem: use Hansen SPA or MCS (stationary bootstrap) or a Holm correction, and treat any variant chosen AFTER seeing test results as exploratory. Nested ablations (model with extra features vs without) under a fixed-parameter view would need Clark-West; under the GW view (forecasts from a given estimation scheme) plain DM-type tests are acceptable.
split_scheme: Not applicable to the papers. Implications for us: the frozen model (fixed estimation at 2026-07-27) vs a rolling baseline is exactly the GW setting (forecasts from different estimation schemes, estimation noise included). The weekly-refit row (D-014) is a different forecast and needs its own paired test against recent-rate on the same rows. Coroneo-Iacone show DM is over-sized with few out-of-sample observations unless fixed-smoothing asymptotics are used; with 33 days / 5 weeks we are in that regime for daily and weekly blocks.
metrics: Test statistics and outputs: DM t statistic and p-value (two-sided, and one-sided 'model better'); HLN-adjusted t; GW Wald chi-square with q degrees of freedom; bootstrap percentile CI for the mean Brier difference and for BSS = 1 - mean(BS_model)/mean(BS_ref) (resampling paired losses keeps the ratio correct); bootstrap P(diff < 0); sign/random-walk test on per-day or per-week wins; SPA p-value and MCS membership for many variants.
unit_of_metric: Pooled over all eligible rows, with inference clustered on time (hour, day or week across all units). Per-unit DM tests are possible but have few positives per unit and should be multiplicity-corrected; per-group (Kyiv City / frontline / rear) tests are the sensible subset level (panel DM 'clusters of units').
baseline_strength: Not a baseline paper. Key point for us: the reference in the test should be the strongest baseline, which is the rolling recent-rate (D-021). Testing against a weak baseline (raw persistence, BSS -0.72 vs recent-rate in our test) gives trivially significant results and says nothing about whether the model is useful.
calibration: Not addressed by DM/GW. A significant Brier gain can come from discrimination or calibration; combine the test with the CORP decomposition (see scoring_rules_corp) so the README can say why the model wins or loses. A DM test can also be applied to the calibration-in-the-large gap if needed, using the same block scheme.
calibration_under_drift: GW is the natural tool for drift questions: an instrument such as 'weeks since cut-off' or 'recent activity level' tests whether relative performance changes over the test window. In our check the per-week Brier difference (model minus recent-rate) was +0.0018, +0.0034, +0.0026, -0.0004, -0.0049 for the weeks starting 27 Jul, 3 Aug, 10 Aug, 17 Aug, 24 Aug: the frozen model lost in the first three weeks and won in the last two. By recent-rate level tercile (hour-level means): low -0.0018, mid -0.0007, high +0.0041, i.e. the model loses mainly in high-activity hours. These are descriptive; see headline_results for the formal tests.
uncertainty_of_gain: Main subject of this entry. Recommended for us: a paired, time-clustered test of the Brier difference vs rolling recent-rate, with (i) a circular or stationary block bootstrap over forecast hours with all 24 units kept together, block length fixed in advance (24h primary; 72h and 168h sensitivity), (ii) a calendar-day block bootstrap, (iii) a week-block bootstrap only as a sensitivity row because we have 5 week-blocks, and (iv) a DM t statistic on the hourly cluster series with Newey-West lag 24 and HLN-style t(T-1) critical values. Our illustrative numbers show the iid-row standard error (0.000589) understates the time-clustered HAC standard error (0.000897 at lag 24, 0.00105 at lag 72) by a factor of about 1.5-1.8; even hour-clustering alone (lag 0, 0.000677) widens it by about 1.15x.
regime_coverage: Not applicable to the papers. For us: the test window (33 scored days, late Jul - Aug 2026) contains no major regime shift; the Sep-2026 yellow/red reform is outside it and its API data must not be mixed into the same test (CLAUDE.md). A DM/bootstrap CI on the new-regime check (D-015 (b)) is possible but must be computed separately and labelled exploratory. The GW framework is the principled way to ask 'is the gain stable across regimes', using an instrument that marks regime or activity level.
leakage_handling: Not a pipeline. Inference-specific leakage and snooping risks: (1) Choosing the block length, HAC lag, or test variant after seeing which gives the smallest p-value; fix them in the plan / preregistration before scoring. (2) Selecting the best of several post-hoc variants on the test (reports/improve/variants_test_posthoc.csv: V2 offset +0.017, V4 weekly refit + offset +0.020 BSS) and then reporting a DM p-value for the winner: the p-value ignores the selection and is invalid; use SPA/MCS across all variants tried, or treat as exploratory. (3) GW instruments that use the current hour's outcome or labels not yet matured at t. (4) Bootstrap that resamples rows independently across units within an hour, which breaks the cross-sectional dependence and gives falsely narrow intervals. (5) Treating the test-set y_bar or a test-fitted recalibration as a reference forecast.
test_window_hygiene: Not applicable to the papers. For us: the final test was first accessed 2026-10-13 00:16 UTC (reports/final_test_access.json) with preregistration hashes. The illustrative check in this entry only re-analyses the already-scored frozen predictions (no model selection, no refit), so it does not change the frozen headline. If the project adopts a bootstrap CI (D-013 item 6), the scheme, block lengths, B and seed should be written into the plan and the README should say it was specified after the first scoring, as an inference-only addition.
headline_results: Literature: (1) DM 1995: a simple test of equal expected loss for any loss and non-Gaussian, serially and contemporaneously correlated errors; asymptotically normal. (2) HLN 1997: DM over-rejects in small samples and multi-step horizons; the HLN correction with t(T-1) fixes much of it. (3) GW 2006: conditional predictive ability tests that are valid with rolling windows and nested models and answer 'which forecast is better for the next period given what we know'; later critique (Zhu & Timmermann 2020) shows possible size distortions and argues the GW null is incompatible with rolling estimation. (4) Diebold 2015: DM is for comparing forecasts, not models. (5) Gilleland et al. 2018: iid tests are badly sized when forecasts are serially correlated and correlated with each other; Hering-Genton was the most robust, dependence-aware bootstraps work but need large samples. (6) Panel DM 2024: a strong common component in loss differentials across units invalidates cross-sectional averaging; cluster on time. (7) Coroneo-Iacone 2020: fixed-smoothing asymptotics give correctly sized DM tests with few out-of-sample observations; the SPF advantage over a random walk was partly spurious. OUR ILLUSTRATIVE CHECK (this researcher's computation on reports/official/test_predictions.csv, 13,116 rows, 791 hours, 33 days; frozen model vs rolling recent-rate, Brier): mean Brier 0.089027 vs 0.088140, difference +0.000887 (model worse), BSS -0.0101. iid-row z = 1.51 (p = 0.13). Hour-clustered DM: lag 0 z = 1.31 (p = 0.19); lag 24 z = 0.99 (p = 0.32); lag 72 z = 0.85 (p = 0.40); lag 168 z = 0.87 (p = 0.38). Lag-1 autocorrelation of the hourly cluster series is only 0.015, so most of the extra width comes from longer-range dependence and cross-sectional clustering. Bootstrap 95% CIs for BSS (B = 4,000, seed 20261017): iid hours [-0.026, +0.005]; circular block 24h [-0.031, +0.010]; 72h [-0.033, +0.013]; 168h [-0.029, +0.010]; stationary mean 24h [-0.031, +0.010]; calendar-day blocks (33) [-0.029, +0.008]; week blocks (5) [-0.033, +0.018]. Bootstrap P(model better) = 0.10-0.22 depending on scheme. Sign test: model better on 12 of 33 days (p = 0.16); better in 12 of 24 units. GW test (hour-level, instruments const + recent-rate level + disagreement + lagged 24h mean d): W = 10.3, q = 4, p = 0.036 with lag 24 (p = 0.005 with lag 0); with const + recent-rate level only, p = 0.20 [uncertain: exploratory, four instrument sets tried, so not multiplicity-corrected; hour-level equal-weight version]. Interpretation (hypothesis): the frozen model is statistically indistinguishable from recent-rate overall (not beaten, not beating), with a 95% CI for BSS of roughly -0.03 to +0.01; relative performance may be predictable from activity level and recent relative performance, which is consistent with D-014 refit or a model/baseline blend, but this was not tested out of sample. The 95% CI half-width of about 0.02 BSS means even the post-hoc V4 gain (+0.020) would be borderline, and it is invalid as inference because V4 was selected on the test.
code_available: Yes, widely. Python: statsmodels.tsa.stattools.diebold_mariano_test(y, forecast_a, forecast_b, lags=None, criterion='mse', harvey_adj=False, horizon=1) (single series only; for our panel, pass the hourly cluster series or compute by hand); arch.bootstrap StationaryBootstrap, CircularBlockBootstrap, MovingBlockBootstrap (docs mark MBB 'not recommended'), optimal_block_length, and arch.bootstrap SPA, StepM, MCS (NCSA licence [uncertain]); 'scores' package DM with Hering-Genton option. R: forecast::dm.test (HLN modified), verification::predcomp.test (DM and Hering-Genton), multDM / MCS packages. Neither statsmodels nor arch is in the project venv; a 40-line numpy/scipy implementation (as in this check) needs no new dependency. The illustrative scripts were written to the session scratchpad only and were not committed.
takeaways_for_project:
1) Answer to 'is the gain over recent-rate real?': on the official frozen test it is not a gain at all. BSS = -0.010, and every dependence-aware scheme gives a 95% CI of roughly [-0.03, +0.01] that contains zero. The honest README statement is 'the frozen model is statistically indistinguishable from the rolling recent-rate baseline on the official test (BSS -0.010, 95% block-bootstrap CI about -0.031 to +0.010, 24h blocks)'. That supports the D-021 wording that not beating recent-rate is a valid result.
2) Implement D-013 item 6 as a paired, time-clustered bootstrap: resample whole time blocks with all 24 units kept together; resample PAIRED losses (lm, lr) per block, and compute diff = sum(lm - lr)/sum(N) and BSS = 1 - sum(lm)/sum(lr) per replicate. Never compare two separate CIs (one per forecaster): the errors are positively correlated because both use recent onsets.
3) Change the planned block from 'week' to 'day' (or 24h circular/stationary) as primary, with week blocks as sensitivity. Reason: the scored test is only 33 days (27 Jul -> 28 Aug 22:00 UTC) because the gap and feature-lookback mask remove 29 Aug -> 7 Sep, leaving 5 uneven week-blocks; a 5-block percentile bootstrap is lumpy. This needs the human's approval since D-013 says 'week-block'. Also correct any README text that calls the scored test '6 weeks'.
4) Report a DM t statistic on the hourly cluster series with Newey-West lag 24 (and 72 as sensitivity) and t(T-1) critical values, next to the bootstrap CI. Fix lag, block lengths, B and seed in the plan before running (preregistration spirit). The iid-row SE is about 1.5-1.8x too small, so never report a row-level paired t-test.
5) The rate ratio form matters: masking gives uneven units per hour, so linearise the ratio (u_t = (D_t - dbar N_t)/Nbar) for DM and resample (lm, lr, N) sums for the bootstrap, so the bootstrap target equals the reported pooled BSS (ratio of mean Briers, consistent with metric_table()).
6) Post-hoc variants (reports/improve: V2 +0.017, V4 +0.020) cannot be tested with DM on the same test: they were chosen after seeing test results. Either run Hansen SPA / MCS over all variants tried (needs arch or a hand-rolled stationary bootstrap) or label them exploratory and wait for fresh data (monthly re-evaluation, M6) for a confirmatory test. A +0.02 BSS gain is about the size of the CI half-width, so even a clean test would be borderline.
7) Use a GW-style conditional test (or simply a preregistered split) to ask 'when does the model beat recent-rate?' with instruments known at t (recent activity level, weeks since cut-off). Our exploratory result (model worse in high-activity hours, better in quiet hours; worse in weeks 1-3, better in weeks 4-5) is a hypothesis that motivates D-014 refit or a blend, not a finding.
8) For the new-regime check (D-015 (b)), compute a separate paired block-bootstrap CI on API data, labelled exploratory, never pooled with the official test (CLAUDE.md). Per-group CIs (Kyiv City, frontline, rear) use the same time blocks; Kyiv City alone has 709 rows and 87 positives, so expect very wide intervals and say so.
9) Do not add statsmodels or arch without approval; numpy/scipy suffice. Put the inference code in src/evaluate.py with a unit test (e.g. a synthetic panel with a common shock where the iid SE is known to be too narrow, plus a test that the bootstrap BSS equals the point BSS at B = 1 with identity resampling).
best_practices: ADOPT: (a) Paired tests on the loss differential, on identical rows, against the strongest baseline (rolling recent-rate). (b) Cluster on time: aggregate to forecast hours across all units, then HAC or block-resample over time; the panel-DM result is that common shocks across units break cross-sectional averaging. (c) Block length chosen by a rule fixed in advance (24h primary, 72h/168h sensitivity; or Politis-White with the 2009 correction), and stated in the README. (d) Small-sample care: HLN t(T-1) or fixed-b critical values when there are few independent blocks. (e) Report the CI of the BSS from resampled paired sums, plus P(diff < 0), plus a simple sign/random-walk count of winning days or weeks as an intuitive check. (f) Multiple-comparison control (SPA, MCS, Holm) whenever more than one variant is compared on the same test. (g) Conditional (GW) analysis only with instruments known at t, labelled exploratory unless preregistered. (h) Say clearly that DM compares forecasts, not models (Diebold 2015). AVOID: (1) iid row-level t-tests or iid row bootstraps on clustered spatio-temporal events. (2) Comparing two marginal CIs instead of the paired difference. (3) Week-block bootstraps with only 5 blocks presented as precise. (4) Choosing block length, lag or test after seeing results. (5) Reporting a p-value for a variant selected on the same test. (6) Restricting evaluation to outcome-selected subsets (forecaster's dilemma). (7) Pooling official and API rows in one test. (8) Treating 'not significant' as 'equal': report the CI so readers see the plausible range of gain or loss.
